languages.name: C
languages.summary: Portable systems programming language created at Bell Labs for Unix; a small, manually memory-managed, statically typed procedural language standardized by ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14 and the lingua franca of operating systems, runtimes and foreign-function interfaces.

level_notes.0: No reference implementation: GCC and Clang/LLVM are the dominant compilers; TinyCC, chibicc, lcc and cproc are small readable ones; CompCert is a formally verified compiler. The standard library is a separate project (glibc, musl, ...).
level_notes.1: The ISO/IEC 9899 standard is paywalled. The freely available WG14 working drafts are linked instead: N3220 (first draft after C23, practically identical to it), N1570 (C11) and N1256 (C99). Section deep links use the HTML rendering of N3220 hosted at port70.net, whose anchors are the standard's clause numbers.
level_notes.2: cppreference.com (a community-maintained reference that paraphrases the standard) is treated as level 2; it answers 403 to automated clients, so those links are reported as 'blocked' by the checker.
level_notes.3: Wikipedia has separate articles for syntax, data types, the standard library and each standard revision.

languages.name: C++
languages.summary: Multi-paradigm systems language that grew out of C with classes: deterministic destruction (RAII), templates and concepts, zero-overhead abstractions, and an ISO standard revised every three years (C++11 ... C++26). Implemented independently by GCC, Clang and MSVC.

level_notes.0: No reference implementation: the three major independent implementations are GCC (g++ front end in gcc/cp, libstdc++), Clang/LLVM (clang/, libc++, libc++abi) and MSVC (compiler closed, STL open). Source links point at the main/master/trunk branches and can move as the projects refactor.
level_notes.1: The ISO/IEC 14882 standard is paywalled. The working draft is public: eel.is/c++draft is an HTML rendering of the current draft (now the C++26 working draft) with stable [section.name] URLs; timsong-cpp.github.io/cppwp/nNNNN hosts frozen drafts per standard (n4861 = C++20, n4950 = C++23). WG21 papers (Pnnnn/Nnnnn at open-std.org) are the proposal record. The Itanium C++ ABI is a separate, de-facto binary standard.
level_notes.2: isocpp.org and cppreference.com refuse automated clients from the checking sandbox (reported 'blocked'); their URLs are long-standing and were kept.
level_notes.3: cppreference.com is filed under level 3 (community wiki summarising the standard) although practitioners use it as the everyday reference.

languages.name: CSS
typing: dynamically checked at parse and computed-value time
languages.summary: Declarative stylesheet language of the web: rules pair selectors (patterns over the document tree) with property declarations, and the cascade, inheritance and per-module layout algorithms turn them into presentation. Defined today as a large family of independently levelled W3C modules rather than one versioned specification.

level_notes.0: No reference implementation. The definition is exercised by the three browser style/layout engines (Blink, Gecko with Servo's Stylo, WebKit), by standalone parsers (rust-cssparser, PostCSS, CSSTree, Lightning CSS, tinycss2), layout libraries (Taffy) and by the shared web-platform-tests suite; the Bikeshed spec sources in w3c/csswg-drafts are listed as tooling. Chromium source is linked on chromium.googlesource.com because the GitHub mirror rate-limits raw fetches.
level_notes.1: There is no single "CSS specification" after CSS 2.1: the language is the set of modules listed in the current CSS Snapshot. Deep links point at the CSSWG editor's drafts (drafts.csswg.org / drafts.css-houdini.org), whose section anchors match the dated W3C TR publications; www.w3.org/TR links are the normative published versions.
level_notes.2: MDN is treated as secondary (explains the specs). Formal-semantics work on CSS layout is academic (Cassius, Meyerovich & Bodik) and listed here rather than at level 1 because it is not part of the definition.
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code has no meaningful CSS category; compatibility tables (caniuse, web-features) play the role of comparison tables.

languages.name: Elixir
languages.summary: Dynamic functional language on the Erlang VM (BEAM) with Erlang's actor-style processes and OTP, a macro system based on quoted expressions, protocols for polymorphism, and a gradual set-theoretic type system being added incrementally.

level_notes.0: There is one implementation: elixir-lang/elixir. The bootstrap compiler is written in Erlang (lib/elixir/src: tokenizer, yecc grammar, expander, translation to Erlang abstract format) and the rest of the language (Kernel macros, type checker, standard library, Mix, ExUnit, IEx) in Elixir itself. Execution relies on erlang/otp (BEAM emulator, scheduler, per-process GC), so key OTP files are linked too.
level_notes.1: No formal specification or standard exists; the reference implementation and its versioned documentation on hexdocs.pm (Syntax reference, Operators, Patterns and guards, Typespecs, Kernel.SpecialForms) define the language. Language changes are proposed on the elixir-lang-core mailing list rather than through numbered RFCs. hexdocs.pm/elixir/* currently redirects to elixir.hexdocs.pm/*.

languages.name: F#
languages.summary: Functional-first, strongly typed ML-family language for .NET with type inference, discriminated unions, pattern matching, computation expressions, units of measure and type providers; also compiles to JavaScript via Fable.

level_notes.0: dotnet/fsharp holds the only full compiler (fsc/fsi, FSharp.Compiler.Service) and FSharp.Core. Pipeline: lex.fsl -> LexFilter (offside rule) -> pars.fsy -> SyntaxTree -> Checking (type inference, constraint solving) -> TypedTree -> Optimizer -> IlxGen -> AbstractIL writer. Fable reuses the front end and emits JavaScript and other targets.
level_notes.1: The F# Language Specification (community-maintained at fsharp.github.io/fslang-spec, continuing the F# 4.1 PDF) is the normative text; features added since 4.1 are specified by fslang-design RFCs, and the Microsoft Learn language reference is the official reference manual. No ISO/ECMA standard.

languages.name: Go
languages.summary: Statically typed, garbage-collected compiled language from Google with CSP-style concurrency (goroutines and channels), structural interfaces and a deliberately small specification.

level_notes.1: No ISO/ECMA standard. The Go Programming Language Specification plus the Go Memory Model are normative; gc (cmd/compile) and gccgo are independent implementations of that spec.
level_notes.0: The main toolchain 'gc' lives in golang/go (compiler in src/cmd/compile, runtime in src/runtime). go/parser, go/ast and go/types in the standard library are a second, library-form front end.

languages.name: Haskell
languages.summary: Purely functional, non-strict (lazy) language with Hindley-Milner type inference extended by type classes; defined by the Haskell 2010 Report and, in practice, by GHC and its many language extensions.

level_notes.0: GHC is the de-facto implementation; its pipeline is Lexer.x/Parser.y -> renamer (GHC/Rename) -> type checker (GHC/Tc) -> desugarer (GHC/HsToCore) -> Core optimiser -> STG -> Cmm -> native/LLVM/JS/Wasm back ends, with the runtime system in rts/. The canonical repository is gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc; links use the official github.com/ghc/ghc mirror. Hugs, MicroHs and UHC are independent implementations.
level_notes.1: The Haskell 2010 Language Report is the last committee standard (no ISO/ECMA standard). Modern Haskell is defined by the GHC User's Guide 'Language extensions' chapter and by accepted GHC proposals; System FC (docs/core-spec) is the formal core calculus.
level_notes.2: Real World Haskell (book.realworldhaskell.org) was unreachable from the research sandbox and is therefore not linked.
level_notes.3: The taxonomy has no 'monads' concept; monad material is tagged purity/input-output/statements (do-notation) where that is what the section covers.

languages.name: HTML
languages.summary: The markup language of the World Wide Web. Since 2019 the WHATWG HTML Living Standard is the single authoritative definition; it specifies the element vocabulary and content models, the DOM-based data model, and an exact error-tolerant parsing algorithm (tokenizer state machine plus tree-construction insertion modes).

level_notes.0: HTML is defined by a specification, not an implementation, but the parsing chapter is an executable algorithm, so parsers are near-transliterations of it. Listed: html5lib (the first implementation, with the shared html5lib-tests corpus), web-platform-tests (the conformance suite), html5ever, parse5, the Gecko/Blink/WebKit/Ladybird parsers, several library parsers, the Nu Html Checker (RELAX NG schemas for document conformance) and the spec source itself. The html5lib-tests tree-construction files are linked as a directory because raw file fetches of that path fail from the research sandbox.
level_notes.1: The WHATWG HTML Living Standard is normative (W3C ceased publishing a competing HTML in 2019; see the MOU). Section numbers in titles drift as the standard changes; the fragment ids are stable. Historical versions (the 1992 "HTML Tags" note, RFC 1866, HTML 3.2, HTML 4.01, W3C HTML5) are included for history. w3.org answers some automated clients with 403, so those links may show as blocked in the link checker; they were verified manually.
level_notes.2: MDN and web.dev are the main maintained tutorials/references; Simon Pieters' "Idiosyncrasies of the HTML parser" is the standard secondary text on the syntax and parser.

languages.name: Java
languages.summary: Statically typed, class-based, garbage-collected language compiled to JVM bytecode. It is defined by two vendor specifications maintained through the Java Community Process and OpenJDK: the Java Language Specification (source language) and the Java Virtual Machine Specification (class files and execution).

level_notes.0: OpenJDK (openjdk/jdk) is the reference implementation: javac lives in src/jdk.compiler, the HotSpot VM in src/hotspot and the class library in src/java.base. Independent implementations include the Eclipse compiler (ECJ), Eclipse OpenJ9 and GraalVM. The TCK (JCK) that decides conformance is not open source; jtreg tests in the OpenJDK tree are the public stand-in.
level_notes.1: No ISO/ECMA standard. The JLS and JVMS (one edition per Java SE release, produced by a JSR) are normative; language changes arrive as JEPs, often first as preview features (JEP 12). The Java SE API specification is the third normative part of a Java SE platform release.
level_notes.2: Oracle's dev.java tutorials supersede the older 'Java Tutorials' (frozen at JDK 8) which are still widely cited.

languages.name: JavaScript
languages.summary: Dynamically typed, prototype-based language with first-class functions, created for Netscape Navigator and standardized as ECMAScript (ECMA-262); it runs in every web browser and in server/embedded runtimes such as Node.js, Deno, Bun and QuickJS.

level_notes.0: There is no reference implementation; ECMA-262 is implemented independently by V8 (Chrome, Node.js), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari), QuickJS, Hermes and others. engine262 mirrors the specification text clause by clause, and test262 is the official conformance suite. SpiderMonkey links use the mozilla-firefox/firefox GitHub repository.
level_notes.1: ECMA-262 is published yearly by Ecma International (also adopted as ISO/IEC 16262); the living draft at tc39.es/ecma262 is the authoritative text between editions. Changes go through the staged TC39 proposal process. Host features (event loop, workers, DOM, Node.js modules) are specified outside ECMA-262.
level_notes.2: MDN is treated as secondary: it is the de-facto reference but is not normative.

languages.name: JSON Schema
languages.summary: Declarative, JSON-encoded vocabulary for describing, annotating and validating JSON documents; a schema is a set of keyword constraints (assertions, applicators, annotations) applied to an instance, with URI-based identification and referencing of subschemas.

level_notes.0: There is no single reference implementation. The official JSON-Schema-Test-Suite is the de-facto conformance suite and the Bowtie harness reports every implementation's results against it; ajv (JavaScript, compiles schemas to code), python-jsonschema, Hyperjump, santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema (Go), jsonschema-rs and networknt (Java) are widely used independent validators.
level_notes.1: Published as a series of IETF Internet-Drafts that never became RFCs ('draft-04', 'draft-06', 'draft-07', '2019-09', '2020-12'); the dialect meta-schemas are normative companions. Since 2022 the project has decoupled from the IETF process and is preparing a self-published stable release (see the ADRs in json-schema-spec).
level_notes.2: 'Understanding JSON Schema' (hosted on json-schema.org) is the standard book-length guide; learnjsonschema.com documents every keyword of every dialect.

languages.name: JSON
languages.summary: Minimal text format for structured data derived from JavaScript literal syntax: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false and null. Defined twice (RFC 8259 / STD 90 and ECMA-404), deliberately unversioned, and the lingua franca of web APIs and configuration.

level_notes.0: JSON has no reference implementation: json.org's JSON_checker and Crockford's json2.js are historical reference code, and nst/JSONTestSuite is the de-facto conformance corpus. Level 0 therefore samples widely used parsers/serializers in many host languages, with files tagged by the part of the format they implement (lexing, number conversion, string escaping, UTF-8 validation, duplicate keys, depth limits).
level_notes.1: Two co-equal normative texts: RFC 8259 (IETF STD 90; grammar in ABNF plus interoperability guidance) and ECMA-404 (syntax only, railroad diagrams; also published as ISO/IEC 21778). They are intended to describe the same language. ECMA-262's JSON.parse/JSON.stringify, I-JSON (RFC 7493) and JCS (RFC 8785) are linked as normative profiles; JSON Pointer/Patch/Path and JSON Schema have their own catalog entries.
level_notes.2: Much of the secondary literature is about interoperability hazards (numbers, duplicate keys, invalid Unicode) and about parser engineering (SIMD, on-demand parsing).
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code has a JSON task rather than a category.

languages.name: Kotlin
languages.summary: Statically typed language from JetBrains targeting the JVM, JavaScript, WebAssembly and native code, with null-safe types, declaration-site variance, extension functions, data/sealed classes and compiler-supported coroutines. Its K2 compiler front end (FIR) feeds a shared IR used by all back ends.

level_notes.0: One implementation: JetBrains/kotlin (K2 front end = PSI parser + FIR; back ends for JVM bytecode, JS, Wasm and Kotlin/Native via LLVM share the 'IR' tree). The repository is too large for directory listings here, so links point at individual files on master. Coroutine library machinery lives in Kotlin/kotlinx.coroutines.
level_notes.1: No ISO/ECMA standard. The Kotlin language specification (kotlinlang.org/spec, source in Kotlin/kotlin-spec) is the normative description of Kotlin/Core; it lags the compiler, so KEEP proposals (Kotlin/KEEP, branch main, files named KEEP-nnnn-*.md) and the compiler define newer features.
level_notes.2: The official documentation at kotlinlang.org/docs is explanatory (guide/tour style) and is filed at level 2; only its keyword table and grammar reference are filed at level 1.

languages.name: OCaml
languages.summary: Statically typed ML-family language from Inria with Hindley-Milner type inference, algebraic data types and pattern matching, a powerful module system (signatures, functors, first-class modules), a structural object system and, since OCaml 5, shared-memory parallelism (domains) and effect handlers. Compiles to bytecode and native code.

level_notes.0: The Inria distribution (ocaml/ocaml: ocamlc bytecode compiler, ocamlopt native compiler, C runtime) is the reference implementation and effectively the definition. js_of_ocaml, Melange and OxCaml reuse its front end; camlboot is an independent bootstrap interpreter.
level_notes.1: There is no standard or formal specification of full OCaml. Part II of 'The OCaml Manual' (the language reference, with BNF) is the authoritative prose description; language changes go through ocaml/RFCs and pull requests against the compiler. Formal semantics exist only for subsets (OCaml light) and for individual features (objects, modules, effects, the memory model).
level_notes.2: Part I of the official manual is a tutorial and is listed at level 2. Real World OCaml and the Cornell CS 3110 textbook are the main free books.

languages.name: PHP
languages.summary: Dynamically typed, reference-counted scripting language originally designed for server-side web templating, with a class-based object model, runtime-enforced type declarations and an RFC-driven evolution process; the Zend Engine in php-src is the reference implementation.

level_notes.0: php-src is the reference implementation: the Zend Engine (Zend/) holds the re2c scanner, Bison grammar, AST compiler, opcode VM (zend_vm_def.h is the template from which the executor is generated), GC and object model; ext/ holds the standard library, ext/opcache the optimizer and JIT. HHVM (see hack), PeachPie (.NET), KPHP and JPHP are alternative implementations of PHP dialects.
level_notes.1: No formal standard. The PHP Language Specification (php/php-langspec, rendered at phplang.org) was written by Facebook/Rex Jaeschke for PHP 5.6/7.0 and is no longer kept current; the php.net Language Reference plus accepted RFCs (wiki.php.net/rfc) describe the current language, and php-src behaviour is definitive.
level_notes.2: No HOPL paper; the manual's History chapter is the main first-party history.
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code reports 'blocked' to automated checkers.

languages.name: Python
languages.summary: Dynamically typed, garbage-collected general-purpose language with indentation-based block structure, a large standard library and optional (gradual) type annotations; defined by the Python Language Reference and the PEP process, with CPython as the reference implementation.

level_notes.0: CPython (C) is the reference implementation: PEG grammar in Grammar/python.gram, compiler and bytecode interpreter in Python/, built-in types in Objects/; its InternalDocs/ directory documents the internals. PyPy (RPython, meta-tracing JIT), MicroPython, GraalPy, Jython, IronPython and RustPython are independent implementations.
level_notes.1: No ISO/ECMA standard. The Python Language Reference and Library Reference (docs.python.org) are normative together with accepted PEPs; the static type system has its own specification at typing.python.org. Where the reference is silent, CPython behaviour is the de facto definition.
level_notes.2: The official Tutorial and HOWTOs are level 2; there is no HOPL paper, so Guido van Rossum's 'History of Python' blog and the Design and History FAQ serve as history sources.
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code reports 'blocked' to automated checkers from the research sandbox.

languages.name: R
languages.summary: Dynamically typed, lazily evaluated, vector-oriented language and environment for statistical computing and graphics; an open-source dialect of S with Scheme-style lexical scoping, first-class environments and several object systems (S3, S4, reference classes).

level_notes.0: GNU R (developed in Subversion, mirrored at wch/r-source) is the reference implementation and the de-facto definition. Alternative implementations: FastR (GraalVM), Renjin (JVM), pqR, Ř/RIR (research JIT), webR (GNU R on WebAssembly).
level_notes.1: No standard or formal specification. The 'R Language Definition' manual is officially still a draft; together with R Internals, Writing R Extensions and the per-function help pages it is the primary description. There is no numbered proposal process: R Core decides, with discussion on R-devel and Bugzilla. The Core R semantics in Morandat et al. (ECOOP 2012) is the main formalisation.
level_notes.2: 'An Introduction to R' is the official tutorial; Advanced R is the standard deep treatment of the language itself.

languages.name: Rust
languages.summary: Systems programming language that guarantees memory and data-race safety without a garbage collector through ownership, borrowing and lifetimes, combined with traits, algebraic data types, pattern matching and zero-cost abstractions.

level_notes.0: rustc (rust-lang/rust) is the reference implementation and de facto definition; it contains the compiler (compiler/), the standard library (library/) and the UI test suite (tests/ui). Alternative implementations: gccrs (GCC front end), mrustc (bootstrapping compiler without borrow checking), rustc_codegen_cranelift and rustc_codegen_gcc (alternative back ends); Miri is an interpreter for MIR that detects undefined behaviour.
level_notes.1: There is no ISO/ECMA standard. The Rust Reference is the official but explicitly incomplete and non-normative language reference; accepted RFCs define individual features; the Ferrocene Language Specification (FLS, adopted by the Rust project in 2025) is a specification written for compiler qualification. Formal models (RustBelt, Stacked/Tree Borrows, Oxide, MiniRust, a-mir-formality) cover parts of the language.
level_notes.2: The official book ('The Rust Programming Language'), Rust by Example and the Rustonomicon are tutorials/guides and therefore level 2; the rustc dev guide is the internals guide.

languages.name: Scala
languages.summary: Statically typed language from EPFL that fuses object-oriented and functional programming on the JVM (also JavaScript via Scala.js and native code via Scala Native). Scala 3 (the Dotty compiler) adds enums, givens/using clauses, union and intersection types, inline/macros metaprogramming and optional-braces syntax, with the DOT calculus as its formal foundation.

level_notes.0: scala/scala3 holds the Scala 3 compiler (dotc), TASTy tooling and the Scala 3 library; scala/scala holds the Scala 2.13 compiler (nsc) and the 2.13 standard library that Scala 3 still uses. Scala.js and Scala Native are alternative back ends with their own IRs.
level_notes.1: No external standard. The Scala Language Specification exists for 2.13 and, partially updated, for 3.4; for Scala 3 features the official 'Scala 3 Reference' is in practice the authoritative text, and the compiler is the final arbiter. Changes go through the Scala Improvement Process (SIPs). The DOT calculus papers give a machine-checked core.
level_notes.2: docs.scala-lang.org hosts the official Scala 3 Book and the older Tour of Scala; 'Programming in Scala' (1st ed.) is free online.

languages.name: PostgreSQL SQL dialect
languages.summary: The SQL dialect of PostgreSQL: a highly standard-conforming, extensible SQL with user-defined types, operators, index access methods and procedural languages, rich built-in types (arrays, ranges, JSONB), CTEs, window functions, MVCC transactions with serializable snapshot isolation, and descent from Berkeley POSTGRES/PostQUEL.
standards: ISO/IEC 9075:2023 (core conformance target; see Appendix D of the manual)

level_notes.0: One implementation defines the dialect: postgres/postgres (parser in src/backend/parser with the Bison grammar gram.y, planner in src/backend/optimizer, executor in src/backend/executor). Level 0 also lists independent re-implementations and extractions of the dialect's grammar (libpg_query, CockroachDB's sql.y, ANTLR, sqlglot, sqlfluff, sqlparser-rs).
level_notes.1: The PostgreSQL manual (Part II 'The SQL Language' and Part VI 'Reference') is the normative description of the dialect; ISO/IEC 9075 is paywalled, so the ISO catalogue page, Appendix D (conformance) and free BNF extractions are linked. The Berkeley POSTGRES design papers are the defining papers of the system's data model and rule/extension design.
level_notes.2: The official tutorial (Part I) and the manual's Internals part are filed here, with books and courses on internals.
level_notes.3: Encyclopedia and catalogue pages; Rosetta Code only has a generic SQL category.

languages.name: SQLite SQL dialect
languages.summary: The SQL dialect of the embedded SQLite library: a large subset of standard SQL with dynamic (per-value) typing, type affinity, a single-file database format and a bytecode virtual machine (VDBE) that every statement is compiled to.

level_notes.0: The canonical source lives in a Fossil repository at sqlite.org/src; github.com/sqlite/sqlite is the official read-only mirror linked here. The parser is generated by Lemon from src/parse.y; every statement is compiled to VDBE bytecode executed by src/vdbe.c.
level_notes.1: There is no specification separate from the implementation: the 'SQL As Understood By SQLite' pages on sqlite.org (with railroad syntax diagrams), the file-format document and the C-API reference are the normative description, and the test suites (TCL tests, sqllogictest, proprietary TH3) are the conformance evidence.
level_notes.2: sqlite.org itself publishes much of the best explanatory material (query planner, atomic commit, architecture); these are listed as level 2 guides/internals guides.

languages.name: TypeScript
languages.summary: A statically checked, structurally and gradually typed superset of JavaScript from Microsoft whose types are erased at compile time; the compiler (tsc) type-checks and emits plain ECMAScript.
standards: ECMA-262 (runtime semantics of the JavaScript it erases to)

level_notes.0: Two official implementations: the original self-hosted compiler written in TypeScript (src/compiler on the release-6.0 branch of microsoft/TypeScript, the last JavaScript-based line) and the native Go port that became TypeScript 7 (microsoft/typescript-go). swc, esbuild, Babel and oxc only parse and strip types; they do not type-check.
level_notes.1: There is no maintained specification: the TypeScript Language Specification was last updated for TypeScript 1.8 (2016) and is archived in the repository. Current behaviour is defined by the compiler, per-release notes, the design goals/notes in the TypeScript wiki and, for runtime semantics, ECMA-262.
level_notes.2: The TypeScript Handbook is official but explanatory (it explicitly is not a specification), so it is filed at level 2.
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code reports 'blocked' to automated checkers.

languages.name: XML
typing: schema-typed (DTD attribute types, external schema languages)
languages.summary: A simplified profile of SGML standardised by the W3C: a Unicode text syntax for labelled trees of elements, attributes and character data, with entities, DTD validation, and a family of companion specifications (Namespaces, Infoset, XInclude, xml:id, canonicalization). The substrate of XHTML, SVG, SOAP, office formats and countless configuration and interchange vocabularies.

level_notes.0: No reference implementation exists; conformance is defined by the W3C/NIST/OASIS XML Conformance Test Suite. The dominant parsers are linked: libxml2 and Expat (C), Xerces (Java/C++, also inside the JDK), plus the standard-library parsers of Python, Go, .NET and several Rust/JS/OCaml implementations that differ in which optional features (DTD, external entities, namespaces) they implement.
level_notes.1: XML 1.0 Fifth Edition is the normative core; it embeds the DTD language (catalogued separately as `dtd`). www.w3.org answers this catalog's link checker with HTTP 403 (reported `blocked`); every W3C anchor below was verified by fetching the page with a different client. Namespaces, Infoset, XML Base, xml:id, XInclude and Canonical XML are separate Recommendations layered on the core; XSD, RELAX NG, XPath, XSLT and XQuery have their own catalog entries.
level_notes.2: Secondary literature is vast but much of the classic material (IBM developerWorks, Sun, Cover Pages) has moved or vanished; surviving canonical items (Bray's Annotated XML, Harold's books, TEI's Gentle Introduction, platform parser guides, security cheat sheets) are linked.
level_notes.3: Wikipedia has separate articles for most sub-topics (namespaces, DTD, CDATA, entity attacks), linked individually because they are section-level tertiary sources.

languages.name: YAML
languages.summary: Human-oriented data serialization language with indentation-based block structure, a JSON-compatible flow syntax, anchors/aliases for shared and cyclic nodes, and tags resolved through schemas. Ubiquitous as a configuration format.

level_notes.0: There is no single reference implementation. libyaml (C, YAML 1.1) underlies PyYAML, Psych and many bindings; yaml-reference-parser is generated mechanically from the 1.2 spec productions; yaml-test-suite is the shared conformance corpus that implementations are compared against (matrix.yaml.info).
level_notes.1: The YAML 1.2.2 specification (yaml.org) is normative; many deployed parsers still implement YAML 1.1 with its larger implicit-typing rules, so the 1.1 spec and the 1.1 type repository are linked as well. RFC 9512 registers the media type.
level_notes.2: Much secondary literature is implementation- or tool-specific (PyYAML, Ansible, Kubernetes/Helm); critical essays on implicit typing are included because they explain the 1.1/1.2 differences.
